extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, playwrights and theorists of comedy and wit
extracted.subtask_description: A theoretical analysis of the fundamental devices that produce the comic in actions, situations, and language; explains mechanisms (repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference) and how they map onto verbal wit. Useful for writers, dramatists, and scholars seeking principles for creating or analysing comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation, that is, a combination of circumstances, which recurs several times in its original form and thus contrasts with the changing stream of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetitions are more laughable the more complex and more naturally introduced the repeated scene is—two conditions the playwright must reconcile. Repetition can be the same characters in different surroundings or different characters reproducing the same incident (e.g., masters then servants). Classic comedy makes repetition seem natural through characters' constant forces/moods; contemporary comedy often prepares the audience directly so an extraordinary coincidence is accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverse the situation and invert the roles (topsyturvydom)—put low in high place or vice versa so that roles recoil on their author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: prisoner lecturing the magistrate, child teaching parents, the villain who is victim of his own villainy. Inversion may be only mentally present (we see only one scene but infer the inverted counterpart). The 'robber robbed' is a stock motif; inversion produces comedy by having a scheme rebound on its originator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference of series
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation is comic when it belongs simultaneously to two altogether independent series of events and is capable of being interpreted in two entirely different meanings at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes equivocal/misunderstanding situations where each character interprets only one series and the audience perceives both. Laughter arises from the revelation of the coincidence of independent series and the author's continual reminder of their independence (e.g., threat of dissolving the partnership repeatedly averted). Interference can be between present/past series, a principal comedy and a smaller comedy inside it, or other pairings (examples: Tartarin manacled to Bonivard; mock-heroic transpositions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisation of life / absentmindedness in events
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy seeks to obtain a mechanisation of life—treating life as if it were a repeating, reversible, interchangeable mechanism; the ludicrous in events is defined as absentmindedness in things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Light comedy exaggerates natural rigidity/absentmindedness into an artform. Because absentmindedness in events is exceptional and slight, comedy depends on convention to amplify it; this mechanisation is a deliberate aesthetic aim rather than mere reportage of real life. The effect is fragile and game-like; character comedy penetrates deeper into life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: comic expressed vs comic created by language
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic EXPRESSED (translatable cases) vs the comic CREATED by language, which 'owes its entire being to the structure of the sentence or to the choice of the words' and is often untranslatable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic created by language is not merely language conveying comic actions but language itself becoming comic through syntax, word-choice or verbal mechanism. To analyse wit one should map verbal effects onto the same comedic categories used for actions and situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit versus Comic (audience/target distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A word is comic when it makes us laugh at the person who utters it, and witty when it makes us laugh either at a third party or at ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit (esprit) in the broader sense is a dramatic way of thinking—seeing ideas converse like persons and creating miniature comic scenes; in the restricted sense wit is the volatile, distilled form of the comic. To analyse a witty remark, expand it into the full scene and classify its comic category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three laws of comic transformation of sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences become comic by the same three operations as events: (1) repetition/transposition, (2) inversion, (3) reciprocal interference of series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inversion (e.g., subject/object swap) is least interesting but commonly used. Reciprocal interference yields puns and true verbal double-meanings (play upon words). Transposition (repetition applied to language) is the most far-reaching: transferring ideas into a different stylistic key so language itself plays a comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurd idea fitted into a well-established phrase-form
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic meaning is invariably obtained when an absurd idea is fitted into a well-established phrase-form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ready-made phrase-forms signal automatism; inserting an absurdity exposes that automatism and makes the phrase comic (examples: M. Prudhomme's sayings). The absurdity is not the sole source of comic effect but a clear means to reveal mechanical utterance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literalisation of metaphor / shifting attention to the physical meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic effect is obtained whenever we pretend to take literally an expression which was used figuratively; once attention is fixed on the material aspect of a metaphor, it becomes comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: turning 'all the arts are brothers' into literal kinship, or exploiting gender mismatch in metaphor to produce comic incongruity. Witty rejoinders often materialise metaphors to trap the interlocutor into producing a comic image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference in language: pun vs play upon words
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal interference of two sets of ideas in the same sentence produces verbal comedy. The pun relies on identical sound for two different sentences; a true play upon words uses a single sentence to express two independent meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pun is the least reputable form (homophony-based); the play upon words more cleanly exploits polysemy or literal/figurative tension. Both betray a momentary lapse or negligence in language and are sources of wit/comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition (verbal repetition / stylistic transfer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposition is to ordinary language what repetition is to comedy: transfer ideas into a different style or key while maintaining mutual relations so the language itself becomes comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You need not present both original and transposed expressions; the effect arises when ideas are made to speak in an alien stylistic setting (e.g., lofty diction about trivial things). This device is especially far-reaching for producing comic contrasts in speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadvertent automatism / use of ready-made phrase-forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Saying or doing what one has no intention of saying due to inelasticity or momentum—language contains ready-made formulas and stereotyped phrases that, when uttered automatically, become comic if they embody an evident absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A phrase must bear signs of automatism to be comic detached from its speaker. Examples include commonplace hygienic prescriptions inverted ('I don't like working between meals') or juxtaposed clichés that hide an absurdity until attention is aroused.
